docs.title: Home
docs.text: cgcnn2 is a reproduction of crystal graph convolutional neural network (CGCNN) for predicting material properties. This documentation will help you get started with using CGCNN for your materials science research.

• Training a CGCNN model using a custom dataset.
  • Predicting material properties with a pre-trained CGCNN model.
  • Fine-tuning a pre-trained CGCNN model on a new dataset.
  • Extracting structural features as descriptors for downstream tasks.

docs.title: Installation Steps
docs.text:
It is recommended to first check your available CUDA version (or CPU only) and install PyTorch following the instructions on the PyTorch official website. Then, you can simply install cgcnn2 from PyPI using pip:

pip install cgcnn2

or, if you manage your project with uv:

uv add cgcnn2

If you'd like to use the latest unreleased version on the main branch, you can install it directly from GitHub:

pip install git+https://github.com/jcwang587/cgcnn2@main

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Network (CGCNN) is a deep learning framework designed for predicting material properties based on their crystal structures. It was introduced in the paper "Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks for an Accurate and Interpretable Prediction of Material Properties".

docs.title: Graph Representation
docs.text:
The main idea in CGCNN is to represent the crystal structure by a crystal graph that encodes both atomic information and bonding interactions between atoms. A crystal graph \(\mathcal{G}\) is an undirected multigraph which is defined by nodes representing atoms and edges representing connections between atoms in a crystal.

Each node \(i\) is represented by a feature vector \(v_i\), encoding the property of the atom corresponding to node \(i\). Similarly, each edge \((i,j)_k\) is represented by a feature vector \(u_{(i,j)_k}\) corresponding to the \(k\)th bond connecting atom \(i\) and atom \(j\).

The crystal graph is unlike normal graphs since it allows multiple edges between the same pair of end nodes, a characteristic for crystal graphs due to their periodicity, in contrast to molecular graphs.

docs.title: Graph Neural Network
docs.text:
The convolutional neural networks built on top of the crystal graph consist of two major components: convolutional layers and pooling layers. The convolutional layers iteratively update the atom feature vector \(v_i\) by "convolution" with surrounding atoms and bonds with a nonlinear graph convolution function,

\[ v_i^{(t+1)} = \text{Conv}\left(v_i^{(t)}, v_j^{(t)}, \mathbf{u}_{(i,j)_k}\right), \quad (i,j)_k \in \mathcal{G}. \tag{1} \]

After \(R\) convolutions, the network automatically learns the feature vector \(v_i^{(R)}\) for each atom by iteratively including its surrounding environment. The pooling layer is then used for producing an overall feature vector \(v_c\) for the crystal, which can be represented by a pooling function,

\[ v_c = \text{Pool}(v_0^{(0)}, v_1^{(0)}, \ldots, v_N^{(0)}, \ldots, v_N^{(R)}) \tag{2} \]

that is invariant under permutations of atom indices and independent of the choice of unit cell. In this work, a normalized summation is used as the pooling function for simplicity, but other functions can also be used. In addition to the convolutional and pooling layers, two fully connected hidden layers with the depths of \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are added to capture the complex mapping between crystal structure and property. Finally, an output layer is used to connect the \(L_2\) hidden layer to predict the target property \(\hat{y}\).

graph LR
    A[Embed] --> B[Conv] --> C[Pool] --> D[L1] --> |softplus| E[L2] --> F[Out]
    E --> |softmax| G[Out]

docs.title: Convolutional Layer
docs.text:
The convolutional operation in CGCNN can be expressed as:

\[ v_i^{(t+1)} = v_i^{(t)} + \sum_{j,k} \sigma\left(z_{(i,j)_k}^{(t)} W_f^{(t)} + b_f^{(t)}\right) \odot g\left(z_{(i,j)_k}^{(t)} W_s^{(t)} + b_s^{(t)}\right) \tag{3} \] \[ z_{(i,j)_k}^{(t)} = v_i^{(t)} \oplus v_j^{(t)} \oplus u_{(i,j)_k} \tag{4} \]

where:

  • \(v_i^{(t)}\) is the feature vector of atom \(i\) at layer \(t\)
  • \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid function (gate)
  • \(g\) is the softplus activation function for introducing nonlinear coupling between layers
  • \(\odot\) is the element-wise multiplication
  • \(\oplus\) is the concatenation operation
  • \(z_{(i,j)_k}^{(t)}\) is the concatenation of the feature vectors of atom \(i\), atom \(j\), and the \(k\)th bond between atom \(i\) and atom \(j\) at layer \(t\)
  • \(W_f^{(t)}\) and \(b_f^{(t)}\) are the learnable weights and biases for the sigmoid function
  • \(W_s^{(t)}\) and \(b_s^{(t)}\) are the learnable weights and biases for the softplus function

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text: Here's a basic tutorial on going through the prediction script using the functions provided by the package.

docs.title: 1. Importing the package
docs.text:
There are three main modules available in the package:

  • cgcnn2.data: For loading and preprocessing the data.
  • cgcnn2.model: Building blocks for the CGCNN model.
  • cgcnn2.utils: Some utility functions.
from cgcnn2.data import CIFData, collate_pool
from cgcnn2.model import CrystalGraphConvNet
from cgcnn2.utils import cgcnn_test

docs.title: 2. Data Preparation
docs.text:
To input material structures into CGCNN, you need to define a custom dataset. Before doing so, make sure you have the following files:

  • CIF files recording the structures of the materials you wish to study.
  • Target properties for each material (not needed for prediction jobs).

Organize these files in a directory (root_dir) with the following structure:

  1. id_prop.csv (optional for prediction): A CSV with two columns, the first column is a unique material ID, and the second column is the corresponding target property value.
  2. atom_init.json: A JSON file that provides the initialization vector for each element. You can use the example at /cgcnn2/asset/atom_init.json from the original CGCNN repository; it should work for most applications.
  3. CIF files: One .cif file per material, named ID.cif, where ID matches the entries in id_prop.csv.

Once your root_dir (for example, examples/data/sample-regression) contains these files, you can load the dataset using the CIFData class:

dataset = CIFData("examples/data/sample-regression")

This will prepare your crystal structures (and, if provided, their target properties) for use with CGCNN. Then, we can build a torch.utils.data.DataLoader object that can be used to load the dataset in a batch.

from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

loader = DataLoader(
    dataset,
    batch_size=args.batch_size,
    shuffle=False,
    num_workers=args.workers,
    collate_fn=collate_pool,
)

docs.title: 3. Model Loading
docs.text:
A checkpoint holds the model weights and the hyperparameters of the architecture, so the model is rebuilt from the checkpoint and the dataset, which provides the input feature lengths:

import torch
from cgcnn2.utils import load_checkpoint, model_from_checkpoint

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
checkpoint = load_checkpoint("formation-energy-per-atom.pth.tar")
model = model_from_checkpoint(checkpoint, dataset).to(device)

Checkpoints contain only tensors and plain Python values, so they load with the default weights_only=True; only load checkpoint files from sources you trust.

docs.title: 4. Prediction
docs.text:
cgcnn_test writes the predictions to a CSV file and, when the dataset has an id_prop.csv, logs the MAE, MSE and R² and saves a parity plot:

cgcnn_test(
    model, loader, device, results_file="results.csv", plot_file="parity_plot.png"
)

For downstream analysis in Python, cgcnn_pred loads the dataset and the model in one call and returns the predictions and the crystal descriptors (the atom features after the convolutions, averaged over each crystal) as NumPy arrays; it writes no files and computes no metrics:

from cgcnn2.pretrained_models import FORMATION_ENERGY_MODEL
from cgcnn2.utils import cgcnn_pred

predictions, descriptors = cgcnn_pred(
    FORMATION_ENERGY_MODEL, "examples/data/sample-regression"
)

Both arrays follow the order of id_prop.csv, or the sorted IDs of the CIF files when there is none.

docs.title: Training Options
docs.text:
You can view the training hyperparameters by using the --help flag with both the cgcnn-tr and cgcnn-ft commands. Most of the hyperparameters are shared between these two scripts, including:

  • batch-size: Specifies the number of samples that are grouped together and processed in one forward/backward pass during both training and fine-tuning. At each step, the DataLoader will pull batch-size examples from the dataset, feed them through the model, compute the loss, and then perform a gradient update. Choosing the right batch-size involves a trade-off between memory usage, computational efficiency, and optimization dynamics. By default, we set batch-size = 256 as a balance between speed and memory requirements on modern GPUs. If you run into OOM errors, try reducing this value; if you have excess memory and want to speed up training, experiment with increasing it.

  • learning-rate: Determines the step size used by the optimizer to update model weights at each gradient step. A higher learning rate makes larger jumps in parameter space, potentially speeding up initial convergence but risking instability or divergence. A lower rate yields more precise, stable updates at the cost of slower training. By default, we set learning-rate = 1e-2 as a good starting point for most graph-based models. If loss oscillates or diverges, try reducing it; if training stalls, consider increasing it or adding a scheduler.

  • epoch: Specifies how many epochs the training loop will make over the entire dataset during both training and fine-tuning. More epochs give the model more opportunities to learn but increase total runtime and can lead to overfitting if too many are used. The default is epoch = 1000. Monitor your validation loss and use early stopping if you observe that performance plateaus.

  • device: The torch device used for the model, e.g. cpu, cuda, cuda:1 or mps. By default cuda is used when it is available, otherwise cpu.

docs.title: Targets and Checkpoints
docs.text:
Targets are standardized internally with the mean and standard deviation of the training set, so one learning rate suits properties of any unit and scale. The loss is the mean squared error on the standardized targets. After every epoch the model is evaluated on the validation set, and the checkpoint with the lowest validation MAE is kept. The statistics are folded into the output layer of the saved checkpoint, so a checkpoint predicts directly in the units of your data and needs nothing else at prediction time.

With --bias-temperature, every error in the loss and in the validation MAE is weighted by exp(-target / bias_temperature), which favors structures with low targets such as low energies. The checkpoint is then selected by this weighted MAE.

docs.title: Early Stopping
docs.text:
Both the training and fine-tuning scripts implement an early stopping strategy that halts training when the validation MAE has not reached a new best for a specified number of consecutive epochs.

  • stop-patience: Defines how many consecutive epochs without a new best validation MAE are allowed before training is terminated. Default is None, which means no early stopping.

docs.title: Learning Rate Scheduler
docs.text:
There is a learning rate scheduler for the training and finetuning scripts, which applies the ReduceLROnPlateau strategy. The default parameters are:

  • factor: The factor by which the learning rate will be reduced. new_lr = lr * factor
  • patience: How many epochs to wait before reducing the learning rate.

You can check more details in the PyTorch documentation.

docs.title: Retraining on Matbench
docs.text:
The bundled models are trained with the recipe below on Matbench datasets, which are fixed and versioned and are fetched through matminer, which is not a dependency of cgcnn2. The four tasks below correspond to the bundled formation-energy-per-atom, band-gap, bulk-moduli and shear-moduli models, whose test errors are listed in the models README; the last column is the 5-fold mean of the CGCNN entry on the Matbench leaderboard.

Task Target Unit Structures Download Leaderboard CGCNN matbench_mp_e_form formation energy eV/atom 132,752 167 MB MAE 0.0337 matbench_mp_gap PBE band gap eV 106,113 137 MB MAE 0.2972 matbench_log_kvrh bulk modulus, log10 log10(GPa) 10,987 4 MB MAE 0.0712 matbench_log_gvrh shear modulus, log10 log10(GPa) 10,987 4 MB MAE 0.0895

examples/matbench_dataset.py writes a task as train/, valid/ and test/ directories in the CIFData layout (<id>.cif files, id_prop.csv and atom_init.json). The test set is the Matbench fold-0 test split, KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=18012019), so a test error corresponds to the fold-0 score of a leaderboard entry. The table lists 5-fold means, and a single fold scatters around its mean. The validation set is a random 10% of the fold-0 training split. IDs follow the Matbench convention, e.g. mb-log-kvrh-00006.

uv run --with matminer examples/matbench_dataset.py matbench_log_kvrh data/matbench_log_kvrh

(or pip install matminer and run the script with python). matminer caches the downloaded file in its package directory unless MATMINER_DATA points elsewhere; writing the 132,752 CIF files of matbench_mp_e_form takes about two minutes. Training and evaluation then use the regular commands: cgcnn-tr evaluates the best checkpoint on the test set when training ends, and cgcnn-pr re-evaluates any checkpoint on it. Both write the per-structure predictions as CSV and a parity plot annotated with the MAE, the leaderboard metric, to output_<job-id>/. A 30-epoch smoke test:

cgcnn-tr --train-set data/matbench_log_kvrh/train --valid-set data/matbench_log_kvrh/valid --test-set data/matbench_log_kvrh/test --epoch 30 --job-id kvrh
cgcnn-pr --model-path output_kvrh/best_model.ckpt --full-set data/matbench_log_kvrh/test --job-id kvrh_test

docs.title: Full runs on a single GPU
docs.text:
Blackwell GPUs such as the RTX 5080 need a PyTorch build with CUDA 12.8 or newer. The default Linux wheels on PyPI qualify; on Windows the PyPI wheel is CPU-only, so install PyTorch from the CUDA index first (pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128). The model has about 100k parameters, so 16 GB of GPU memory is far more than --batch-size 256 needs; the run is bound by CIF parsing and Python data loading instead, and --workers decides where that cost goes:

  • --workers 0 (default): the dataset's LRU cache keeps every parsed crystal graph in RAM, so each CIF is parsed once, during the first epoch. The cache costs about 3 KB per atom: 0.3 GB for matbench_log_kvrh and about 11 GB for matbench_mp_e_form (3.9 million atoms).
  • --workers N: the DataLoader re-creates its worker processes every epoch with empty caches, so the whole dataset is re-parsed every epoch (in parallel). Only worth it when RAM is short.
for task in matbench_mp_e_form matbench_mp_gap matbench_log_kvrh matbench_log_gvrh; do
    uv run --with matminer examples/matbench_dataset.py $task data/$task
    cgcnn-tr --train-set data/$task/train --valid-set data/$task/valid --test-set data/$task/test \
        --epoch 1e3 --stop-patience 1e2 --learning-rate 1e-2 --lr-patience 20 \
        --batch-size 256 --workers 0 --job-id $task --random-seed 42
done

The test MAE of each run is printed on output_<task>/parity_plot.png, with the predictions in output_<task>/test_results.csv.

class AtomInitializer:
    """
    Atom feature vectors read from an `atom_init.json` file, a dictionary mapping
    atomic numbers to feature vectors.

    Args:
        elem_embedding_file (str): Path to the JSON file.
    """

    def __init__(self, elem_embedding_file):
        with open(elem_embedding_file) as f:
            elem_embedding = json.load(f)
        self._embedding = {
            int(number): np.array(vector, dtype=float)
            for number, vector in elem_embedding.items()
        }

    def get_atom_fea(self, atom_type):
        """
        Return the feature vector of an atomic number.

        Args:
            atom_type (int): Atomic number.
        """
        return self._embedding[atom_type]

class CIFData(Dataset):
    """
    Crystal structures stored as CIF files in one directory.

    - `atom_init.json`: the initialization vector of each element.
    - `ID.cif`: one CIF file per crystal, where `ID` is the unique ID of the crystal.
    - `id_prop.csv` (optional): two columns, the ID of each crystal and the value of its
      target property. Without it every CIF file in the directory is loaded with a NaN
      target, which is all that prediction needs.

    Parsed crystal graphs are kept in a per-instance LRU cache, so each CIF file is
    parsed once per process.

    Args:
        root_dir (str): The dataset directory.
        max_num_nbr (int): Maximum number of neighbors per atom in the crystal graph.
        radius (float): Cutoff radius for the neighbor search.
        dmin (float): Center of the first Gaussian of the distance expansion.
        step (float): Spacing of the Gaussian centers.
        cache_size (int | None): Number of parsed crystals kept in memory. None (default)
            keeps all of them, 0 disables the cache.

    Each item is `((atom_fea, nbr_fea, nbr_fea_idx), target, cif_id)`:

        atom_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (n_i, atom_fea_len)
        nbr_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (n_i, M, nbr_fea_len)
        nbr_fea_idx (torch.LongTensor): shape (n_i, M)
        target (torch.Tensor): shape (1,)
        cif_id (str): the ID of the crystal
    """

    _cache_load: Callable[[int], Item]

    def __init__(
        self,
        root_dir: str | os.PathLike[str],
        max_num_nbr=12,
        radius=8,
        dmin=0,
        step=0.2,
        cache_size=None,
    ):
        assert os.path.isdir(root_dir), f"{root_dir} is not a directory"
        self.root_dir = root_dir
        self.max_num_nbr, self.radius = max_num_nbr, radius
        id_prop_file = os.path.join(root_dir, "id_prop.csv")
        if os.path.isfile(id_prop_file):
            with open(id_prop_file) as f:
                self.id_prop_data = [
                    (row[0], float(row[1])) for row in csv.reader(f) if row
                ]
        else:
            self.id_prop_data = sorted(
                (name[:-4], float("nan"))
                for name in os.listdir(root_dir)
                if name.endswith(".cif")
            )
        self.ari = AtomInitializer(os.path.join(root_dir, "atom_init.json"))
        self.gdf = GaussianDistance(dmin=dmin, dmax=radius, step=step)
        self.cache_size = cache_size
        self._configure_cache()

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.id_prop_data)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        return self._cache_load(index)

    def __getstate__(self):
        # The lru_cache wrapper around a bound method is not picklable; drop
        # it so instances survive spawn-based DataLoader workers.
        state = self.__dict__.copy()
        state.pop("_cache_load", None)
        return state

    def __setstate__(self, state):
        self.__dict__.update(state)
        self._configure_cache()

    def _configure_cache(self) -> None:
        if self.cache_size is not None and self.cache_size <= 0:
            self._cache_load = self._load_item
        else:
            self._cache_load = functools.lru_cache(maxsize=self.cache_size)(
                self._load_item
            )

    def _load_item(self, index: int) -> Item:
        cif_id, target = self.id_prop_data[index]
        crystal = Structure.from_file(os.path.join(self.root_dir, f"{cif_id}.cif"))
        graph = _crystal_graph(
            crystal, cif_id, self.ari, self.gdf, self.max_num_nbr, self.radius
        )
        return graph, torch.tensor([target], dtype=torch.float32), cif_id

class GaussianDistance:
    """
    Expands interatomic distances (in angstrom) in a Gaussian basis.

    Args:
        dmin (float): Center of the first Gaussian.
        dmax (float): Center of the last Gaussian.
        step (float): Spacing between consecutive centers.
        var (float | None): Variance of each Gaussian. Defaults to `step`.
    """

    def __init__(self, dmin, dmax, step, var=None):
        assert dmin < dmax
        assert dmax - dmin > step
        self.filter = np.arange(dmin, dmax + step, step)
        self.var = step if var is None else var

    def expand(self, distances):
        """
        Project distances onto the Gaussian basis.

        Args:
            distances (np.ndarray): Interatomic distances of any shape.

        Returns:
            np.ndarray: `distances.shape + (len(filter),)` basis values.
        """
        return np.exp(-((distances[..., np.newaxis] - self.filter) ** 2) / self.var**2)

def batch_to_device(batch, device):
    """
    Move the batch tensors produced by `collate_pool` to a device.

def collate_pool(dataset_list: list[Item]):
    """
    Collate a list of dataset items into one batch.

    Args:
        dataset_list (list): Items `((atom_fea, nbr_fea, nbr_fea_idx), target, cif_id)` as
            returned by `CIFData`, with `n_i` atoms and `M` neighbors per atom.

    Returns:
        tuple: `((atom_fea, nbr_fea, nbr_fea_idx, crystal_atom_idx), target, cif_ids)` where

            - atom_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (N, orig_atom_fea_len), all atoms of the batch
            - nbr_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (N, M, nbr_fea_len), bond features of each atom's neighbors
            - nbr_fea_idx (torch.LongTensor): shape (N, M), neighbor indices into the batch
            - crystal_atom_idx (torch.LongTensor): shape (N,), the crystal of each atom, sorted ascending
            - target (torch.Tensor): shape (B, 1)
            - cif_ids (list[str]): the ID of each crystal
    """
    batch_atom_fea, batch_nbr_fea, batch_nbr_fea_idx = [], [], []
    crystal_atom_idx, batch_target, batch_cif_ids = [], [], []
    base_idx = 0
    for crystal_i, ((atom_fea, nbr_fea, nbr_fea_idx), target, cif_id) in enumerate(
        dataset_list
    ):
        n_i = atom_fea.shape[0]
        batch_atom_fea.append(atom_fea)
        batch_nbr_fea.append(nbr_fea)
        batch_nbr_fea_idx.append(nbr_fea_idx + base_idx)
        crystal_atom_idx.append(torch.full((n_i,), crystal_i, dtype=torch.long))
        batch_target.append(target)
        batch_cif_ids.append(cif_id)
        base_idx += n_i
    return (
        (
            torch.cat(batch_atom_fea),
            torch.cat(batch_nbr_fea),
            torch.cat(batch_nbr_fea_idx),
            torch.cat(crystal_atom_idx),
        ),
        torch.stack(batch_target),
        batch_cif_ids,
    )

def full_set_split(
    full_set_dir: str,
    train_ratio: float,
    valid_ratio: float,
    train_force_dir: str | None = None,
    random_seed: int = 0,
):
    """
    Split a dataset directory into train, valid and test directories.

    The CIF files are copied into three temporary directories that are removed when
    the process exits. The test set receives whatever the two ratios leave.

    Args:
        full_set_dir (str): The dataset to split.
        train_ratio (float): Fraction of the dataset used for training.
        valid_ratio (float): Fraction of the dataset used for validation.
        train_force_dir (str | None): A dataset directory whose structures are all added
            to the training set on top of the split.
        random_seed (int): Seed of the shuffle.

    Returns:
        tuple[str, str, str]: The train, valid and test directories.
    """
    df = pd.read_csv(
        os.path.join(full_set_dir, "id_prop.csv"),
        header=None,
        names=["cif_id", "property"],
    )
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_seed)
    df = df.sample(frac=1.0, random_state=rng).reset_index(drop=True)
    n_train, n_valid = int(len(df) * train_ratio), int(len(df) * valid_ratio)
    splits = [
        [(df[:n_train], full_set_dir)],
        [(df[n_train : n_train + n_valid], full_set_dir)],
        [(df[n_train + n_valid :], full_set_dir)],
    ]
    if train_force_dir is not None:
        df_force = pd.read_csv(
            os.path.join(train_force_dir, "id_prop.csv"),
            header=None,
            names=["cif_id", "property"],
        )
        splits[0].append((df_force, train_force_dir))

    temp_dirs = []
    for parts in splits:
        temp_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
        atexit.register(shutil.rmtree, temp_dir, ignore_errors=True)
        for part, source_dir in parts:
            for cif_id in part["cif_id"]:
                shutil.copy(os.path.join(source_dir, f"{cif_id}.cif"), temp_dir)
        pd.concat([part for part, _ in parts]).to_csv(
            os.path.join(temp_dir, "id_prop.csv"), index=False, header=False
        )
        shutil.copy(os.path.join(full_set_dir, "atom_init.json"), temp_dir)
        temp_dirs.append(temp_dir)
    return tuple(temp_dirs)

class ConvLayer(nn.Module):
    """
    Crystal graph convolution: updates the features of every atom from its
    neighbors and the bonds to them.

    Args:
        atom_fea_len (int): Number of hidden atom features.
        nbr_fea_len (int): Number of bond features.
    """

    def __init__(self, atom_fea_len: int, nbr_fea_len: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.atom_fea_len = atom_fea_len
        self.nbr_fea_len = nbr_fea_len
        self.fc_full = nn.Linear(2 * atom_fea_len + nbr_fea_len, 2 * atom_fea_len)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm1d(2 * atom_fea_len)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm1d(atom_fea_len)
        self.softplus = nn.Softplus()

    def forward(
        self,
        atom_in_fea: torch.Tensor,
        nbr_fea: torch.Tensor,
        nbr_fea_idx: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        `N` is the number of atoms in the batch and `M` the number of neighbors per atom.

        Args:
            atom_in_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (N, atom_fea_len), atom features before the convolution.
            nbr_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (N, M, nbr_fea_len), bond features of each atom's neighbors.
            nbr_fea_idx (torch.LongTensor): shape (N, M), indices of each atom's neighbors.

        Returns:
            torch.Tensor: shape (N, atom_fea_len), atom features after the convolution.
        """
        n_atoms, n_nbr = nbr_fea_idx.shape
        # fc_full acts on the concatenation [atom_i, atom_j, bond_ij]. Applying its
        # three weight blocks separately gives the same result while the two atom
        # terms are computed once per atom instead of once per neighbor pair, and
        # the (N, M, 2 * atom_fea_len + nbr_fea_len) concatenation never exists.
        # index_select gathers the neighbor term with a deterministic backward.
        w_self, w_nbr, w_bond = self.fc_full.weight.split(
            [self.atom_fea_len, self.atom_fea_len, self.nbr_fea_len], dim=1
        )
        nbr_term = F.linear(atom_in_fea, w_nbr).index_select(0, nbr_fea_idx.reshape(-1))
        gated_fea = (
            F.linear(atom_in_fea, w_self, self.fc_full.bias).unsqueeze(1)
            + nbr_term.view(n_atoms, n_nbr, -1)
            + F.linear(nbr_fea, w_bond)
        )
        gated_fea = self.bn1(gated_fea.view(-1, 2 * self.atom_fea_len)).view(
            n_atoms, n_nbr, 2 * self.atom_fea_len
        )
        nbr_filter, nbr_core = gated_fea.chunk(2, dim=2)
        nbr_summed = (torch.sigmoid(nbr_filter) * self.softplus(nbr_core)).sum(dim=1)
        return self.softplus(atom_in_fea + self.bn2(nbr_summed))

class CrystalGraphConvNet(nn.Module):
    """
    Crystal graph convolutional neural network for predicting a material property.

    Args:
        orig_atom_fea_len (int): Number of atom features in the input.
        nbr_fea_len (int): Number of bond features.
        atom_fea_len (int): Number of hidden atom features in the convolutional layers.
        n_conv (int): Number of convolutional layers.
        h_fea_len (int): Number of hidden features after pooling.
        n_h (int): Number of hidden layers after pooling.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        orig_atom_fea_len: int,
        nbr_fea_len: int,
        atom_fea_len: int = 64,
        n_conv: int = 3,
        h_fea_len: int = 128,
        n_h: int = 1,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Linear(orig_atom_fea_len, atom_fea_len)
        self.convs = nn.ModuleList(
            [ConvLayer(atom_fea_len, nbr_fea_len) for _ in range(n_conv)]
        )
        self.conv_to_fc = nn.Linear(atom_fea_len, h_fea_len)
        self.fcs = nn.ModuleList(
            [nn.Linear(h_fea_len, h_fea_len) for _ in range(n_h - 1)]
        )
        self.fc_out = nn.Linear(h_fea_len, 1)
        self.softplus = nn.Softplus()

    def forward(
        self,
        atom_fea: torch.Tensor,
        nbr_fea: torch.Tensor,
        nbr_fea_idx: torch.Tensor,
        crystal_atom_idx: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        """
        `N` is the number of atoms in the batch, `M` the number of neighbors per atom
        and `B` the number of crystals.

        Args:
            atom_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (N, orig_atom_fea_len), atom features from the atom type.
            nbr_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (N, M, nbr_fea_len), bond features of each atom's neighbors.
            nbr_fea_idx (torch.LongTensor): shape (N, M), indices of each atom's neighbors.
            crystal_atom_idx (torch.LongTensor): shape (N,), the crystal of each atom, sorted ascending.

        Returns:
            out (torch.Tensor): shape (B, 1), the predicted property.
            crys_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (B, atom_fea_len), the mean atom features of each crystal after the convolutions.
        """
        atom_fea = self.embedding(atom_fea)
        for conv in self.convs:
            atom_fea = conv(atom_fea, nbr_fea, nbr_fea_idx)
        crys_fea = self.pooling(atom_fea, crystal_atom_idx)
        h_fea = self.softplus(self.conv_to_fc(self.softplus(crys_fea)))
        for fc in self.fcs:
            h_fea = self.softplus(fc(h_fea))
        return self.fc_out(h_fea), crys_fea

    def pooling(
        self, atom_fea: torch.Tensor, crystal_atom_idx: torch.Tensor
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Mean-pool atom features into crystal features.

        Args:
            atom_fea (torch.Tensor): shape (N, atom_fea_len), the atom embeddings of the batch.
            crystal_atom_idx (torch.LongTensor): shape (N,), the crystal of each atom, sorted ascending.

        Returns:
            torch.Tensor: shape (B, atom_fea_len), the mean embedding of each crystal.
        """
        n_crystals = int(crystal_atom_idx[-1]) + 1
        index = crystal_atom_idx.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, atom_fea.shape[1])
        return atom_fea.new_zeros(n_crystals, atom_fea.shape[1]).scatter_reduce_(
            0, index, atom_fea, reduce="mean", include_self=False
        )

def cgcnn_test(
    model: torch.nn.Module,
    loader: DataLoader,
    device: torch.device | str,
    results_file: str = "results.csv",
    plot_file: str = "parity_plot.png",
    axis_limits: Sequence[float] | None = None,
    xlabel: str = "Actual",
    ylabel: str = "Predicted",
) -> None:
    """
    Predict over a loader and write the results to a CSV file. When the dataset has
    targets, also log the MAE, MSE and R² and save a parity plot.

    Args:
        model (torch.nn.Module): The model.
        loader (DataLoader): The data, batched with `collate_pool`.
        device (torch.device | str): Where the model lives.
        results_file (str): CSV file receiving `cif_id,true,pred` rows sorted by ID.
        plot_file (str): PNG file receiving the parity plot.
        axis_limits (Sequence[float] | None): `(min, max)` of true values for an
            additional parity plot clipped to that range.
        xlabel (str): x-axis label of the parity plot.
        ylabel (str): y-axis label of the parity plot.
    """
    predictions, _, targets, cif_ids = predict(model, loader, device)
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        {"cif_id": cif_ids, "true": targets, "pred": predictions}
    ).sort_values("cif_id")
    df.to_csv(results_file, index=False)
    logging.info(f"Prediction results have been saved to {results_file}")

    if df["true"].isna().any():
        logging.info("The dataset has no targets; metrics and parity plot are skipped.")
        return
    errors = df["true"] - df["pred"]
    mae = np.mean(np.abs(errors))
    mse = np.mean(errors**2)
    r2 = 1 - np.sum(errors**2) / np.sum((df["true"] - df["true"].mean()) ** 2)
    logging.info(f"MAE: {mae:.4f}, MSE: {mse:.4f}, R2 Score: {r2:.4f}")

    plot_hexbin(df, xlabel, ylabel, out_png=plot_file)
    logging.info(f"Hexbin plot has been saved to {plot_file}")
    if axis_limits is not None:
        low, high = axis_limits
        clipped_file = plot_file.replace(".png", f"_axis_limits_{low}_{high}.png")
        plot_hexbin(
            df[(df["true"] >= low) & (df["true"] <= high)],
            xlabel,
            ylabel,
            out_png=clipped_file,
        )
        logging.info(
            f"Hexbin plot clipped to {axis_limits} on true has been saved to {clipped_file}"
        )

def load_checkpoint(model_path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> dict:
    """
    Load a cgcnn2 checkpoint onto the CPU and log its epoch and validation error.

    Checkpoints hold only tensors and plain Python values, so they are read with
    `weights_only=True`.

    Args:
        model_path (str): Path to the checkpoint file.

    Returns:
        dict: The checkpoint, with the keys `epoch`, `state_dict`, `args` and
            `best_mae_error` (`best_mse_error` in checkpoints trained with 0.6).
    """
    checkpoint = torch.load(model_path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)
    metrics = [
        f"{key[5:8].upper()}={checkpoint[key]:.4f}"
        for key in ("best_mse_error", "best_mae_error")
        if key in checkpoint
    ]
    logging.info(
        f"=> Loaded checkpoint '{model_path}' (epoch {checkpoint.get('epoch', 'N/A')}, "
        f"validation {', '.join(metrics) or 'N/A'})"
    )
    return checkpoint

def metrics_text(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    metrics: Sequence[str] = ("mae", "r2"),
    metrics_precision: str = "3f",
    unit: str | None = None,
    unit_scale: float = 1.0,
) -> str:
    """
    Format metrics of the `true` and `pred` columns of a DataFrame as LaTeX lines.

    Args:
        df (pd.DataFrame): DataFrame with `true` and `pred` columns.
        metrics (Sequence[str]): Any of `mae`, `mse`, `rmse` and `r2`.
        metrics_precision (str): Format spec of the metric values.
        unit (str | None): Unit of the property.
        unit_scale (float): Factor applied to the error metrics.

    Returns:
        str: One line per metric.
    """
    errors = df["true"] - df["pred"]
    values: dict[str, float] = {}
    for m in metrics:
        m_lower = m.lower()
        if m_lower == "mae":
            values["MAE"] = np.mean(np.abs(errors)) * unit_scale
        elif m_lower == "mse":
            values["MSE"] = np.mean(errors**2) * unit_scale**2
        elif m_lower == "rmse":
            values["RMSE"] = np.sqrt(np.mean(errors**2)) * unit_scale
        elif m_lower == "r2":
            values["R^2"] = 1 - np.sum(errors**2) / np.sum(
                (df["true"] - df["true"].mean()) ** 2
            )
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported metric: {m}")

    text_lines: list[str] = []
    for name, val in values.items():
        if name == "R^2":
            text_lines.append(rf"$R^2: {val:.3f}$")
            continue
        unit_str = ""
        if unit:
            unit_str = (
                rf"\,\mathrm{{{unit}}}^2" if name == "MSE" else rf"\,\mathrm{{{unit}}}"
            )
        text_lines.append(rf"$\mathrm{{{name}}}: {val:.{metrics_precision}}{unit_str}$")
    return "\n".join(text_lines)

def model_from_checkpoint(checkpoint: dict, dataset: CIFData) -> CrystalGraphConvNet:
    """
    Build the model described by a checkpoint's `args` and load its weights.

    Args:
        checkpoint (dict): A checkpoint from `load_checkpoint`.
        dataset (CIFData): A dataset built with the same `atom_init.json` and neighbor
            settings as the training data; it provides the input feature lengths.

    Returns:
        CrystalGraphConvNet: The model, on the CPU.
    """
    orig_atom_fea_len, nbr_fea_len = input_feature_lengths(dataset)
    args = checkpoint["args"]
    model = CrystalGraphConvNet(
        orig_atom_fea_len,
        nbr_fea_len,
        atom_fea_len=args["atom_fea_len"],
        n_conv=args["n_conv"],
        h_fea_len=args["h_fea_len"],
        n_h=args["n_h"],
    )
    model.load_state_dict(checkpoint["state_dict"])
    return model

def plot_hexbin(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    xlabel: str,
    ylabel: str,
    ax: plt.Axes | None = None,
    metrics: Sequence[str] = ("mae", "r2"),
    metrics_precision: str = "3f",
    unit: str | None = None,
    unit_scale: float = 1.0,
    subfigure_label: str | None = None,
    out_png: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Draw a hexbin parity plot of the `true` and `pred` columns of a DataFrame.

    Args:
        df (pd.DataFrame): DataFrame with `true` and `pred` columns.
        xlabel (str): Label of the x-axis.
        ylabel (str): Label of the y-axis.
        ax (plt.Axes | None): Axes to draw on; a new figure when None.
        metrics (Sequence[str]): Metrics written on the plot, see `metrics_text`.
        metrics_precision (str): Format spec of the metric values.
        unit (str | None): Unit of the property.
        unit_scale (float): Factor applied to the error metrics.
        subfigure_label (str | None): Label written above the metrics.
        out_png (str | None): PNG file to save the figure to.
    """
    with plt.rc_context(PLOT_RC_PARAMS):
        if ax is None:
            fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6), layout="constrained")
        else:
            fig = ax.get_figure()
            if not isinstance(fig, plt.Figure):
                raise TypeError("`ax` must be attached to a top-level Figure")

        hb = ax.hexbin(df["true"], df["pred"], gridsize=40, cmap="viridis", bins="log")
        ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
        ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
        ax.set_box_aspect(1)

        # y = x reference line over the current limits
        xlim, ylim = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()
        min_val, max_val = min(xlim[0], ylim[0]), max(xlim[1], ylim[1])
        ax.plot([min_val, max_val], [min_val, max_val], "--", color="grey", linewidth=2)
        ax.set_xlim(xlim)
        ax.set_ylim(ylim)

        # density colorbar inside the plot
        cax = inset_axes(
            ax, width="3.5%", height="70%", loc="lower right", borderpad=0.5
        )
        fig.colorbar(hb, cax=cax)
        cax.yaxis.set_ticks_position("left")
        cax.yaxis.set_label_position("left")

        text = metrics_text(df, metrics, metrics_precision, unit, unit_scale)
        if subfigure_label is not None:
            text = f"{subfigure_label}\n{text}"
        ax.text(0.025, 0.975, text, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="top")

        if out_png is not None:
            fig.savefig(out_png, format="png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")

def predict(
    model: torch.nn.Module, loader: DataLoader, device: torch.device | str
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, list[str]]:
    """
    Run a model over a loader.

    Args:
        model (torch.nn.Module): The model.
        loader (DataLoader): The data, batched with `collate_pool`.
        device (torch.device | str): Where the model lives.

    Returns:
        predictions (np.ndarray): shape (n,), the predicted property of each crystal.
        descriptors (np.ndarray): shape (n, atom_fea_len), the mean atom features of each crystal after the convolutions.
        targets (np.ndarray): shape (n,), NaN where the dataset has no targets.
        cif_ids (list[str]): The ID of each crystal.
    """
    model.eval()
    predictions, descriptors, targets, cif_ids = [], [], [], []
    with torch.inference_mode():
        for batch, target, cif_id in loader:
            output, crys_fea = model(*batch_to_device(batch, device))
            predictions.append(output.cpu().numpy().ravel())
            descriptors.append(crys_fea.cpu().numpy())
            targets.append(target.numpy().ravel())
            cif_ids.extend(cif_id)
    return (
        np.concatenate(predictions),
        np.concatenate(descriptors),
        np.concatenate(targets),
        cif_ids,
    )

def standardize_output(
    model: CrystalGraphConvNet, target_stats: tuple[float, float]
) -> None:
    """
    Make a model that predicts in the original units predict standardized targets, by
    rewriting its output layer. `train` needs this for a model loaded from a checkpoint.

    Args:
        model (CrystalGraphConvNet): The model, changed in place.
        target_stats (tuple[float, float]): Mean and standard deviation from `target_statistics`.
    """
    mean, std = target_stats
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.fc_out.bias.sub_(mean).div_(std)
        model.fc_out.weight.div_(std)

def target_statistics(dataset: CIFData) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """
    Mean and standard deviation of the targets of a dataset.

    Args:
        dataset (CIFData): The dataset, usually the training set.
    """
    targets = np.array([target for _, target in dataset.id_prop_data])
    mean, std = float(targets.mean()), float(targets.std())
    if not std > 0:  # NaN without targets, 0 when they are all equal
        raise ValueError(
            "The targets are missing or all equal, so they cannot be standardized."
        )
    return mean, std

def train(
    model: CrystalGraphConvNet,
    train_loader: DataLoader,
    valid_loader: DataLoader,
    optimizer: torch.optim.Optimizer,
    device: torch.device | str,
    epochs: int,
    checkpoint_path: str,
    checkpoint_args: dict,
    target_stats: tuple[float, float],
    scheduler: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau | None = None,
    stop_patience: int | None = None,
    bias_temperature: float = -1.0,
) -> None:
    """
    Train a model and keep the weights with the lowest validation MAE.

    The model is trained on standardized targets, `(target - mean) / std`, so that one
    learning rate suits properties of any unit and scale. A new model can be passed as it
    is; a model that already predicts in the original units, such as one loaded from a
    checkpoint, needs `standardize_output` first. The loss is the mean squared error.

    Checkpoints have the statistics folded into the output layer, so they predict in the
    original units. When training ends the model holds the weights of the best checkpoint.

    Args:
        model (CrystalGraphConvNet): The model, already on `device`.
        train_loader (DataLoader): Training data, batched with `collate_pool`.
        valid_loader (DataLoader): Validation data.
        optimizer (torch.optim.Optimizer): The optimizer.
        device (torch.device | str): Where the model lives.
        epochs (int): Number of epochs.
        checkpoint_path (str): Where the best checkpoint is written.
        checkpoint_args (dict): Stored under the checkpoint's `args` key. It must hold the
            model hyperparameters (`atom_fea_len`, `n_conv`, `h_fea_len`, `n_h`) so that
            `model_from_checkpoint` can rebuild the model.
        target_stats (tuple[float, float]): Mean and standard deviation of the training
            targets, from `target_statistics`.
        scheduler (ReduceLROnPlateau | None): Stepped with the validation MAE every epoch.
        stop_patience (int | None): Epochs without improvement before training stops.
        bias_temperature (float): If positive, every error is weighted by
            `exp(-target / bias_temperature)` in the loss and in the validation MAE, so
            that structures with low targets (low energies) weigh more.
    """
    mean, std = target_stats
    best_valid_mae = float("inf")
    epochs_without_improvement = 0
    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        model.train()
        train_loss = 0.0
        for batch, targets, _ in train_loader:
            targets = targets.to(device)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs, _ = model(*batch_to_device(batch, device))
            loss = (outputs - (targets - mean) / std) ** 2
            if bias_temperature > 0:
                loss = loss * torch.exp(-targets / bias_temperature)
            loss = loss.mean()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            train_loss += loss.item()
        train_loss /= len(train_loader)

        predictions, _, targets, _ = predict(model, valid_loader, device)
        errors = np.abs(predictions * std + mean - targets)
        if bias_temperature > 0:
            errors = errors * np.exp(-targets / bias_temperature)
        valid_mae = float(errors.mean())
        if scheduler is not None:
            scheduler.step(valid_mae)
        learning_rates = [group["lr"] for group in optimizer.param_groups]
        logging.info(
            f"Epoch [{epoch:03d}/{epochs}] - Train Loss: {train_loss:.5f}, "
            f"Valid MAE: {valid_mae:.5f}, LR: {learning_rates}"
        )
        if valid_mae < best_valid_mae:
            best_valid_mae = valid_mae
            epochs_without_improvement = 0
            # fold the target statistics into the output layer: the checkpoint predicts
            # in the original units
            state_dict = dict(model.state_dict())
            state_dict["fc_out.weight"] = state_dict["fc_out.weight"] * std
            state_dict["fc_out.bias"] = state_dict["fc_out.bias"] * std + mean
            torch.save(
                {
                    "epoch": epoch,
                    "state_dict": state_dict,
                    "best_mae_error": valid_mae,
                    "args": checkpoint_args,
                },
                checkpoint_path,
            )
            logging.info(f"  [SAVE] Best model at epoch {epoch}.")
        elif stop_patience is not None:
            epochs_without_improvement += 1
            if epochs_without_improvement >= stop_patience:
                logging.info(
                    f"Early stopping after {stop_patience} epochs without improvement."
                )
                break
    logging.info("Training complete.")
    model.load_state_dict(torch.load(checkpoint_path, weights_only=True)["state_dict"])
